description:
Iris (Iris spp.) is a common ornamental flower that is mildly to moderately toxic to cats. The rhizome, which is the thick underground stem, contains the highest amount of irritating compounds.

Iris plants contain irisin, iridoid glycosides, and related compounds that can irritate the digestive tract. Leaves and petals can also cause symptoms, but the underground rhizome is usually the biggest risk during digging, repotting, or garden work.

If a cat eats iris, possible signs include drooling, vomiting, diarrhea, belly pain, or low energy. Keep rhizomes and plant cuttings away from cats. Call a veterinarian if your cat eats the rhizome, symptoms repeat, or your cat seems very tired.
name: Iris
safetyNotes: Toxic compounds: irisin (resinous glycoside), iridoid glycosides, pentacyclic terpenoids; rhizomes most concentrated
Mechanism: irisin and iridoid compounds cause direct GI irritation; skin contact with sap may cause dermatitis
Symptoms: drooling, vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy, abdominal pain; skin or eye contact with sap may cause redness or irritation
Rhizomes are the most hazardous part — risk increases during planting or dividing bulbs
Symptoms are usually mild with leaf nibbling; contact your vet if rhizome ingestion is suspected

symptoms.name: Vomiting, Nausea, and Diarrhea
symptoms.notes: These are the most common signs of ingestion. The toxicity is highest in the bulbs, so cats digging up or chewing on rhizomes are at greater risk than those nibbling leaves.

symptoms.name: Mouth Ulcers and Oral Irritation
symptoms.notes: Ingestion can cause physical damage and chemical irritation to the mouth, leading to visible sores or ulcers. Drooling (hypersalivation) may occur as a reaction to this irritation.

symptoms.name: Skin Irritation (Dermatitis)
symptoms.notes: Contact with the plant sap or parts can cause irritation to the skin, which is a distinct symptom noted for Irises compared to many other toxic plants.

symptoms.name: Abdominal Pain
symptoms.notes: This pain is likely secondary to the severe gastrointestinal irritation caused by the plant's compounds.Important Distinction: It is crucial to distinguish Iris from True Lilies (Lilium or Hemerocallis species).

treatments.description: If the cat is brought in shortly after ingestion, the veterinarian may administer medication to induce vomiting. This expels the plant material from the stomach before the toxins (irritating resinoids and glycosides) are fully absorbed or pass into the intestines.
treatments.name: Induction of Emesis (Vomiting)
treatments.notes: This is particularly urgent if the cat has ingested the bulb, which contains the highest concentration of toxins and causes the most severe symptoms25. Owners should not attempt to induce vomiting at home, as this can cause injury or aspiration.

treatments.description: The veterinary team administers fluids directly into the bloodstream or under the skin to correct electrolyte imbalances and hydration levels.
treatments.name: Intravenous (IV) or Subcutaneous Fluid Administration
treatments.notes: This treatment is critical because Iris ingestion causes symptoms that lead to rapid fluid loss, including nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea2. Fluid therapy helps maintain blood pressure and supports the body in clearing the toxins.

treatments.description: Veterinarians may administer anti-emetics (to stop vomiting), medications to coat the stomach, and analgesics for pain.
treatments.name: Gastroprotectants and Pain Management
treatments.notes: Iris toxicity is distinct for causing mouth ulcers and oral irritation78. Supportive care is necessary to soothe the chemical burns in the mouth and throat that may prevent the cat from eating or drinking comfortably.

treatments.description: If the cat has plant sap on its fur or skin, the vet may wash the area with mild soap and water to prevent further absorption or ingestion during grooming.
treatments.name: Dermal Washing / Bathing
treatments.notes: Unlike many other toxic plants, the Iris is specifically noted for causing dermatitis (skin irritation) upon contact78. Removing traces of the plant from the coat prevents the cat from re-infecting itself by licking the irritated skin.
